newsitem.title: SPAIN: Basque leaders urge ETA rebels to declare truce.
newsitem.headline: Basque leaders urge ETA rebels to declare truce.

text.p: The government of Spain's Basque region called on ETA guerrillas on Saturday to follow the example of the Irish Republican Army and declare a truce, saying it was time to "put a stop to the killing."
The appeal for an end to ETA's campaign of terror was issued one week after separatist rebels killed town councillor Miguel Angel Blanco and sparked national outrage.
It came on the same day that bells rang out in unison from churches and town halls across Spain in continuing protest against the brutal murder.

Declaring that "the decision is clearly in ETA's hands," Basque leaders issued their plea for the rebels to "silence their weapons" shortly after the IRA announced a new truce to take effect in Northern Ireland on Sunday.
"The public outcry of the past week points precisely in that direction," Basque Interior Minister Juan Maria Atutxa said.

Millions of Spaniards, incensed by the murder of an ordinary, low-ranking functionary, have taken to the streets in recent days to vent their anger. Pope John Paul and other world leaders have also condemned the killing.
Atutxa said ETA was now faced with "an historic moment and a chance to give a future of peace and hope to this people."
"If these intolerant, violent people come to the realization it's time to put a stop to the killing and their crimes ... all democrats will agree to it," he said.
Atutxa urged ETA's political arm, Herri Batasuna, to support the call for a truce just as the IRA's political arm Sinn Fein had backed such a move by the guerrillas in Northern Ireland.
"Every day that passes without a condemnation of ETA's crimes and without support for a truce makes (Herri Batasuna) more of an accomplice to the murders committed," he said.
"The Basque government is calling on ETA and Herri Batasuna to follow the example of what has happened this weekend in Ireland," Atutxa said.
A spokesman for Herri Batasuna declined comment.

The Basque government called for a truce of "indefinite" duration, but a leading Basque nationalist politician, Inaki Anasagasti, said ETA would have to disavow violence for at least a a year to prove its desire for peace was genuine.

The last ETA truce lasted for only one week in the summer of 1996. The rebels ended it after rejecting the government's demand that they renounce violence before any negotiations could take place. The guerrillas then mounted a series of bomb attacks on tourist resorts.
Many Spaniards stood in silence on Saturday as bells rang for five minutes beginning at 4 p.m. in a show of solidarity for Blanco's family and of condemnation for his murderers.

It was timed to mark the one-week anniversary of a crime that has mobililised public opposition in a way never seen in ETA's 29-year history of armed struggle. The group has killed nearly 800 people in its fight for an independent homeland encompassing parts of northern Spain and southern France.

Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar predicted on Friday night that July 12, 1997, would go down in history as a critical turning point in the government's fight against "a terrorist minority dedicated to the destruction of democracy."
Memorial masses were held for Blanco in several cities on Saturday, and scores of people in a town in southern Spain launched a hunger strike described as a protest against "all kinds of terrorism."
A week earlier, ETA ignored the pleas of half a million people who gathered in the Basque city of Bilbao to plead for Blanco's life.
ETA abducted the young politician on July 10 and vowed to kill him in 48 hours unless more than 500 rebel inmates were transferred to the autonomous Basque region. The government refused.
Just after the deadline passed, the rebels shot him twice in the back of the head and dumped him on a roadside outside the northern city of San Sebastian. He died 12 hours later.
